title: Five Notes After 19:00
teaser: Lin Lan was asked to increase evening-course enrollment, and enrollment did rise. But once demand clustered around 19:00, she could move teachers while still having no authority to change the core timetable or the threshold for opening a class. The hardest problem was not getting people through the door, but deciding who should be accountable once they arrived.
paragraphs: At 17:20 on Thursday, the front desk brought fourteen paid registration forms into Lin Lan's office. None of the students had been assigned to a class yet, and nine had checked only one option: after 19:00. The two beginner classes at 19:00 the following week had only scattered seats left. Lin Lan wrote the nine names on sticky notes and placed them along the right side of the timetable. In the past, she had mainly been responsible for class stability, refunds, and budget performance. Within the framework set by headquarters, she could move teachers, merge small classes, and adjust the branch's local schedule. That system was not perfect, but most of the results she carried were still results she could influence with decisions of her own.

Two weeks earlier, headquarters had changed the branch managers' quarterly bonus so that new evening-course enrollment carried much more weight. Demand after work was rising in several cities, and headquarters had launched a national advertising campaign for evening classes at the same time. Lin Lan could still decide on local trial lessons, teacher shifts, and how to use existing seats. Pricing, the advertising rhythm, fixed course times, and the rule that a new class required eighteen students remained centrally controlled. She moved one afternoon teacher into the evening and opened three trial sessions. In the first week, new evening-course enrollment reached nineteen. Empty seats filled quickly, and she wrote '+19' in the upper-right corner of the timetable.

After the third trial lesson, Lin Lan saw that the problem was not total capacity. Demand was piling up specifically around 19:00. She summarized the preferred times from all three sessions and checked the teacher roster. One teacher could take an additional class on Wednesday evening. Lin Lan submitted two options: move one 18:00 class half an hour later, or allow a new 19:00 class to open at fourteen students and fill the remaining seats in the next intake. Headquarters did not simply say no. Standardized times made national scheduling and transfers between branches easier, and the eighteen-student threshold protected the network from running too many persistently inefficient small classes. Both requests therefore had to wait for the next scheduling approval. Lin Lan cancelled the additional local trial sessions that same day, but people who had already attended continued to enroll, and leads from the national campaign kept entering the system.

She did not push classes beyond their capacity, and she did not place an unprepared teacher into a 19:00 slot. What remained was to match students to individual vacancies, rearrange teacher rotations, and explain the waiting order to new students. The number in the upper-right corner moved from '+19' to '+28'. The nine sticky notes disappeared one by one, only for new evening enrollments to replace some of them. By the end of the second week, five people still had no option except to wait for a 19:00 place. One student had already paid and had been waiting for two weeks; in the end, that student asked for a refund. The enrollment target kept improving, while a refund form appeared in the front-desk drawer.

Lin Lan checked teacher hours again. There was still unused teaching time in the afternoon, and the teacher who could take an evening class was still available. If the problem were simply a shortage of people, the branch had not exhausted its resources. At the quarterly meeting, headquarters first saw '+28', then the five waiting-list notes, the refund record, and the two scheduling requests that had not been approved. Data from other branches also showed that standardized times and the eighteen-student threshold still reduced confusion and empty classes in most locations, so no one treated them as bad rules that should simply be removed. The issue was narrower. If Lin Lan was to remain primarily evaluated and rewarded for evening enrollment, she needed at least some decision space over the supply required to serve that demand. If those decisions had to stay centralized, the evaluation system also needed to separate students left unplaced because of central constraints from results the branch could actually control.

In the end, headquarters opened only a limited exception. If demand met the agreed threshold for two consecutive weeks, a branch could request moving one evening slot half an hour later. Quality standards and the class-opening threshold would remain in force during the trial. The performance sheet would also add a separate count for 'students not placed because of central timetable or class-opening rules' instead of treating all unplaced students as a branch-controlled result. After the meeting, Lin Lan folded the timetable back into its folder. '+28' was still there. The 19:00 column was still crowded with names, and five waiting-list notes remained along the right edge.
concept: The 'three-legged stool' view of organizational design focuses on whether decision rights, performance measurement, and rewards fit together. If someone is evaluated and rewarded for a result, that person needs enough relevant decision authority to materially influence it. If key decisions must remain centralized, the resulting outcomes cannot all be treated as locally controllable performance. The point is not that more delegation is always better, but that authority, measurement, and rewards need to be aligned.
explanation: The normal state in the story is that Lin Lan is mainly responsible for class stability, refunds, and budget performance, while also having enough local scheduling tools to influence those outcomes. Headquarters later puts new evening-course enrollment into her bonus calculation but keeps advertising, fixed time slots, and the class-opening threshold centralized. Lin Lan therefore reasonably directs attention toward the levers she can still use: trial lessons and teacher allocation. Enrollment rises from '+19' to '+28'. Once demand concentrates at 19:00, she identifies the problem early, proposes two capacity solutions, and stops adding local trial sessions. This rules out explanations based on poor ability, carelessness, or knowingly expanding after overload was already clear. Waiting lists and a refund appear because the rewarded demand outcome and the adjustable supply decisions no longer move together. Headquarters also has legitimate efficiency reasons for retaining common rules, so the resolution is limited delegation and a clearer definition of controllable performance, not the removal of standards or full decentralization.
mapping: Earlier evaluation focused on class stability, refunds, and budget performance, while Lin Lan could adjust teachers and classes locally → a normal baseline in which decision rights and result responsibility were broadly aligned.

The quarterly bonus shifts toward new evening-course enrollment, while advertising, fixed times, and the eighteen-student class threshold remain centralized → measurement and rewards change before key decision rights do.

Lin Lan uses trial lessons and teacher allocation to reach '+28', then applies for changes and stops adding extra sessions once the 19:00 bottleneck is visible → her behavior is driven by the new evaluation system, not by incompetence, carelessness, or disregard for quality.

Teacher hours remain available in the afternoon, yet 19:00 capacity cannot expand in time under the central rules, leaving five waiting-list notes and one refund → the visible enrollment gain separates from the real service result and exposes the misalignment among the three elements.
boundary: Alignment does not mean pushing pricing, advertising, course standards, or scheduling entirely down to local branches. Central rules may create brand consistency, scale efficiencies, and quality control, and local units do not always have better information or capabilities. Practical responses can include limited exception rights, faster approval, a clearer definition of controllable metrics, or different reward weights. The key questions are who is held responsible for a result, who can actually influence it, and whether rewards are designed around the same boundary of responsibility.
reflection: If the 19:00 timetable and the eighteen-student threshold must remain centrally controlled, which parts of evening enrollment, waiting lists, and refunds should still affect Lin Lan's bonus, and which should not?
